title: VLOOKUP vs INDEX MATCH: which lookup should you use?
intro: Every Excel user hits this fork: keep the one-liner VLOOKUP, or switch to the two-function INDEX + MATCH combo. VLOOKUP is shorter to write; INDEX + MATCH is structurally tougher — it survives column inserts, looks left, and returns positions as well as values.
verdict: Use VLOOKUP for quick, right-looking lookups in stable tables. Use INDEX + MATCH when the return column sits left of the key, when columns may be inserted, or when you need the match position — and if you have Microsoft 365, skip both and use XLOOKUP.

rows.left: No — the lookup column must be leftmost
rows.right: Yes — lookup and return ranges are independent
Yes — ranges move with the data

rows.right: MATCH match_type 1 or -1; same sorting rule
MATCH alone returns the row position
Slightly faster — only scans needed ranges

useLeftWhen: The key column is already leftmost and the table shape is fixed.
You want the shortest possible formula for a one-off lookup.

useRightWhen: The value you want sits left of the lookup column.
Columns get inserted or reordered in the source table.
You need the row position (for OFFSET, INDIRECT or further math).

title: VLOOKUP vs XLOOKUP: is it time to switch?
intro: XLOOKUP was designed to retire VLOOKUP. It defaults to exact match, searches any column in any direction, spills whole rows, and has a built-in 'if not found' argument — the only real blocker is that it requires Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021+.
verdict: If every user of the workbook is on Microsoft 365 / Excel 2021+, use XLOOKUP — it is strictly better. Stay on VLOOKUP (or INDEX + MATCH) when the file must open in Excel 2016 or earlier.

rows.right: Safe — uses ranges, not an index

useLeftWhen: The workbook must run in Excel 2019 or older.
You're editing a legacy file and consistency matters more than features.
useRightWhen: Everyone on Microsoft 365 — exact-match default, left lookups, and no IFERROR wrapper.
You need to return a whole row or search bottom-up for the latest record.

title: SUMIF vs SUMIFS: one condition or many?
intro: SUMIF and SUMIFS differ by more than the trailing S — the argument order flips (the sum range is last in SUMIF, first in SUMIFS), and only SUMIFS accepts more than one criterion. Reach for the plural even with a single condition if you might add filters later.
verdict: Use SUMIF for a single condition and short formulas; use SUMIFS whenever you may need a second criterion — the extended form is identical in power and more future-proof.

rows.right: Every range must match exactly or #VALUE!

useLeftWhen: You have exactly one condition and want the shortest formula.
You're targeting ancient Excel 2003 files.
useRightWhen: You need two or more filters — region AND month AND amount.
The report will grow new criteria; upgrading SUMIF later is fiddly.

title: COUNT vs COUNTA: what does each one actually count?
intro: COUNT and COUNTA answer different questions: COUNT tallies numeric cells only, while COUNTA tallies anything non-empty. Picking the wrong one quietly over- or under-counts — the classic sign is a 'row count' that includes header text or a 'response count' that skips text answers.
verdict: Use COUNT for columns that should be purely numeric (amounts, scores, quantities). Use COUNTA for completeness checks — 'how many rows were filled in'.
useLeftWhen: The column is meant to hold numbers and text there is a data bug.
You're averaging or summing the same range — COUNT stays consistent.
useRightWhen: You want 'how many rows have anything' — form responses, name lists.
The column mixes types on purpose.

title: IF vs IFS: nested branches or a flat list?
intro: One test, two outcomes — IF is perfect. Three or more outcomes — nested IFs get hard to audit fast ('which parenthesis closes which branch?'), and IFS replaces them with a flat test/result list that stops at the first TRUE.
verdict: Use IF for a single binary decision. Use IFS for three-plus branches — but only on Excel 2019 / Microsoft 365; older files need nested IF.
useLeftWhen: There's exactly one condition.
The file must open in Excel 2016 or earlier.
useRightWhen: You have grade bands, status maps or tiered pricing.
Readability matters — auditors can scan IFS top to bottom.

title: CONCAT vs TEXTJOIN: joining text the right way
intro: Both join text — the difference is the delimiter. CONCAT glues items directly together; TEXTJOIN puts a separator between them and can skip empty cells, which is what 'a, b, c' lists and CSV exports actually need.
verdict: Use TEXTJOIN whenever items need a separator or the list may contain blanks; use CONCAT (or just &) when pieces bolt together with nothing between.

rows.right: First argument, applied between every item

useLeftWhen: No separator is needed — 'report' + '2026' + '.xlsx'.
You want to mix literals and ranges freely.
useRightWhen: You're building comma-separated or dashed lists.
Some cells may be empty and you don't want stray delimiters.

title: LEFT vs MID: slicing text from the start or the middle
intro: LEFT takes a fixed-length prefix; MID takes a slice from any position. Many jobs that look like LEFT tasks — 'everything before the dash' — are really MID/FIND territory once the prefix length varies.
verdict: Use LEFT for fixed-width prefixes; use MID (with FIND to locate the start) when the piece you want sits at a variable position.
useLeftWhen: You need the first N characters and N is constant — country codes, prefixes.
useRightWhen: The target sits after a delimiter or at a computed position — domains, middle segments.

title: COUNTIF vs COUNTIFS: counting with one test or several
intro: COUNTIF counts cells matching one criterion; COUNTIFS stacks range/criteria pairs so every test must pass. Unlike SUMIF→SUMIFS the argument order stays the same — criteria always follow their range — so upgrading is painless.
verdict: Use COUNTIF for one condition; use COUNTIFS for anything more — or when the report might gain a second filter later.

title: FILTER vs lookup functions: one match or all of them?
intro: Lookups return the first match and stop; FILTER returns every matching row as a spill range. If your question is 'which rows', not 'which value', you want FILTER — the catch is it needs Microsoft 365.
verdict: Use FILTER when you need all matching rows and you're on Microsoft 365. Use VLOOKUP / INDEX+MATCH for single-cell answers and older Excel versions.

title: INDEX MATCH vs XLOOKUP: which lookup should you use?
intro: INDEX/MATCH and XLOOKUP both overcome VLOOKUP's leftward and column-index limits. XLOOKUP is shorter and easier to read; INDEX/MATCH still works in older Excel versions and can be more flexible in complex workbooks.
verdict: Use XLOOKUP for new Microsoft 365 workbooks because it is simpler. Use INDEX/MATCH when you need compatibility with older Excel or already have helper structures built around it.

You want a built-in default for missing matches.

title: SUMIF vs COUNTIF: should you total or count?
intro: SUMIF and COUNTIF use the same criteria logic but answer different questions. SUMIF adds values; COUNTIF counts rows. Choosing the wrong one is a common cause of reports that are off by a factor or missing totals.
verdict: Use SUMIF when you need a total of matching values. Use COUNTIF when you need the number of matching rows or cells.
useLeftWhen: You need a dollar total, quantity total or hours total for matching rows.
The answer should change when the underlying values change.
useRightWhen: You need to know how many rows meet a condition.
You are checking completeness, errors or backlog counts.

title: SUMPRODUCT vs SUMIFS: conditional totals with or without helper columns?
intro: When you need to total only the rows that meet several conditions, SUMPRODUCT can do it with one range and an array of booleans, while SUMIFS reads like plain English and handles wildcards natively. The catch is that SUMPRODUCT's math semantics and its habit of returning #VALUE! on text in summed ranges trip up people who only copy it from tutorials.
verdict: Use SUMIFS whenever your criteria are simple comparisons (equals, greater than, wildcards) — it is clearer, faster and far more forgiving. Use SUMPRODUCT when you need custom arithmetic in the test, such as 'sum price times quantity for items in Q1', or you are on Excel 2003 where SUMIFS does not exist.

rows.right: Classic conditional total: sum_range plus range/criteria pairs

title: XLOOKUP vs FILTER: one match or every match?
intro: XLOOKUP returns a single value per lookup — or spills a row or column when the return array is two-dimensional — while FILTER returns the entire set of rows that satisfy a condition. Choosing between them is really choosing between 'find this record' and 'list every record that matches'.
verdict: Use XLOOKUP when you look up one key and want the associated value, with exact match by default and a built-in not-found message. Use FILTER when the answer is a list: all rows for a customer, all dates after a cutoff, all products below a price — and it needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021+.

title: IFERROR vs ISERROR: hide the error or test for it?
intro: IFERROR is a wrapper that swaps any error for a value of your choosing, while ISERROR is a test that returns TRUE or FALSE and leaves the error visible. One replaces the symptom, the other exposes it — and that difference matters for auditing and for avoiding masked mistakes.
verdict: Use IFERROR when you want a clean fallback shown to end users, such as a dash for a missing lookup. Use ISERROR (or better, ISNA, ISNUMBER, ISBLANK) when you need to branch on specific error types, count errors, or keep the original formula visible for debugging.

title: SWITCH vs IFS: exact value match or multiple conditions?
intro: SWITCH compares one expression against a list of exact values and returns the result for the first match, while IFS evaluates a chain of independent TRUE/FALSE conditions. SWITCH is elegant for codes and categories; IFS is the general-purpose replacement for nested IFs with no 'else' trap.
verdict: Use SWITCH when you are mapping one value (a status code, grade, region) to a result and exact equality is what you mean. Use IFS when conditions are ranges, comparisons or different cells — and prefer IFS over nested IF whenever you have more than two branches.

title: EOMONTH vs DATE: getting the last day of the month
intro: EOMONTH takes any date and returns the last day of its month, rolling forward or backward with an offset. DATE builds a date from year, month and day numbers and can do the same job with a little arithmetic, but it is not self-documenting and mishandles day zero unless you know the trick.
verdict: Use EOMONTH whenever you need month-end dates, billing cut-offs or month boundaries — it is shorter and safer. Use DATE when you are constructing dates from parts (year, month, day) or need full control such as the first day of next month via DATE(y,m+1,1).

title: TRIM vs CLEAN: spaces and invisible characters
intro: TRIM and CLEAN sound interchangeable but fix different problems: TRIM removes extra spaces (leading, trailing, and repeated internal spaces down to one), while CLEAN strips non-printing control characters such as line breaks and tab codes imported from other systems. Neither one does the other's job.
verdict: Use TRIM for text tidied by eye — extra spaces from copy-paste or concatenation. Use CLEAN for text imported from web pages, PDFs or other spreadsheets that contains invisible control characters. For a really messy import, nest them: CLEAN first, then TRIM.

title: UNIQUE vs Remove Duplicates: formula list or one-time cleanup?
intro: UNIQUE is a dynamic-array formula that returns a de-duplicated list and updates itself when the source changes, while Excel's Remove Duplicates command permanently rewrites the range in place. One is a living view, the other is a destructive edit — and that decides which one belongs in your workflow.
verdict: Use UNIQUE when you want a live, spill-based list that refreshes with the source and can feed COUNT, charts or lookups. Use Remove Duplicates when you are producing a final static dataset for export, pivot tables or another system, and you have backed up the original.

title: RANK vs LARGE: position or value?
intro: RANK tells you where a number sits in a list (1st, 2nd, 3rd) and ties share the same rank with the next rank skipped, while LARGE simply returns the nth biggest value in a range. They answer different questions, and knowing the difference saves you from ranking a value you already have or fetching a value when you only wanted its position.
verdict: Use RANK (or its modern RANK.EQ / RANK.AVG replacements) when you need the position of a specific value in a list, such as a salesperson's standing. Use LARGE when you need the value itself at a position, such as the top three scores, especially inside a dynamic formula like LARGE(range,k).

title: VLOOKUP vs HLOOKUP: vertical or horizontal tables?
intro: VLOOKUP and HLOOKUP are twins: one scans down a column to find a key and returns a value from a column to the right, the other scans across a row and returns a value from a row below. The data layout decides which one you need, and most real-world tables are vertical, which is why VLOOKUP dominates.
verdict: Use VLOOKUP when your lookup key sits in the leftmost column of a normal row-per-record table — the common case. Use HLOOKUP only when your data is genuinely laid out with keys across the top row and values in rows beneath, such as a matrix of monthly figures by category.

rows.right: Rows = fields, columns = periods or categories

rows.right: Row index is harder to keep track of

useRightWhen: Your key values run across the top row (dates, months, versions).
Each field is a row and each period is a column.

title: TODAY vs NOW: date only or date and time?
intro: TODAY returns today's date with a time of 00:00:00, while NOW returns the current date and time, updated whenever the sheet recalculates. Both are volatile, meaning they recalculate on every change, which is why they are fast but can slow down large workbooks if overused.
verdict: Use TODAY when you only need the calendar date — deadlines, ages in days, month-to-date comparisons — because it is stable within a day and easier to reason about. Use NOW only when the time of day matters, such as timestamps, elapsed durations, or SLA deadlines, and prefer a static value or VBA if you need a frozen timestamp.

useRightWhen: You need the current time, such as for a timestamp or duration.
You calculate time remaining in hours or minutes.

title: Absolute vs relative reference: when to lock a cell
intro: Excel references come in three flavours: relative (A1), which moves when copied; absolute ($A$1), which never moves; and mixed ($A1 or A$1), which locks only one axis. The wrong choice is the most common cause of 'the formula worked in row 1 but broke in row 2' bugs.
verdict: Use relative references for values that should move with each row or column when you copy a formula. Use absolute references for constants, lookup tables, tax rates or denominators that must stay fixed. Use mixed references for grids where only the row or only the column should change, such as a multiplication table.

rows.right: Shifts by the same offset as the copy

useRightWhen: Each row or column has its own value that should move with the formula.

title: TEXTBEFORE vs LEFT: split by delimiter or by count?
intro: TEXTBEFORE (and its sibling TEXTAFTER) splits text at a delimiter you specify, returning everything before or after the first occurrence. LEFT simply returns the first n characters. If your data has variable-length fields separated by a delimiter, TEXTBEFORE is the right tool; if you know exactly how many characters you need, LEFT is simpler and works everywhere.
verdict: Use TEXTBEFORE when the position of what you want is defined by a delimiter such as a space, comma, hyphen or @ — especially for names, emails or codes with varying lengths. Use LEFT when you know the exact character count, such as the first three digits of an ID, or when you must support Excel 2019 or older where TEXTBEFORE does not exist.
